Testimony of Anya Trundy, Deputy Commissioner Department of Administrative and Financial Sen/ices
Testifying Neither For Nor Against

LD 774, An Act to Require Bleeding Control Kits in State-owned Buildings

Sponsored by Rep. Chad Perkins Before the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and
Local Government: I am Anya Trundy, Deputy Commissioner for the Department of Administrative and Financial Sen/ices, and I am providing testimony today Neither For Nor Against LD 774, and will request that the Committee amend the bill in several ways.
Under LD 774, DAFS is required to install bleeding control kits, which include materials for tourniquet
application and other items for the treatment of traumatic injury and blood loss. The Department believes that the bill aims to provide an extra layer of safety to those individuals working and visiting State facilities.
DAFS is, of course, supportive of the mission, however, there are no federal mandates requiring these
kits, and OSHA only recommends them for workplaces with a high risk of injury; State office buildings do
not fall into this category. Thus, there doesn't appear to be any authority recommending how bleeding
control kits should be dispersed throughout State facilities based upon building occupancy and/or size.
While rulemaking authority is granted to the Department, we would prefer clarity within the statute as to the priority of placement as well as the standard of maintenance for bleeding control kits. DAFS would
also inquire whether the Committee intends for the bill to apply beyond Executive Branch facilities to the Legislative Branch, Judicial Branch, the UMaine System, Community College System, Maine Maritime Academy, and quasi-governmental entities.
Additionally, LD 774 creates a fund through which DAFS may provide grants or reimbursements to schools, businesses and other organizations that place bleeding control kits on their premises or make available bleeding control training programs. DAFS suggests to the Committee that a more intuitive location for this fund would be under MaineEMS within the Department of Public Safety given that they
interact with the public on this topic via Stop the Bleed training. Additionally, this bill leaves the source of this funding somewhat up-in-the-air, suggesting the funds could be acquired through "appropriations,
allocations or money received through grants, gifts, or donation from public or private sources." MaineEMS would be more likely to seek out and receive grants, gifts or donations for this purpose than DAFS.
Lastly, DAFS does need to identify that this bill will have a fiscal note for initial implementation costs as
well as ongoing maintenance costs. Depending on the occupancy and size of a given building, multiple kits could be required where other facilities would be sufficiently equipped with one. Additionally, kits

Dear Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government:

The members of the Maine Chapter of the American College of Surgeons ask for your support for L.D. 774(H.P.497), which proposes installing bleeding control kits in state-owned buildings across Maine. As constituents and concerned members of our community, we believe ensuring the safety and well-being of the public is a top priority, and this bill represents a crucial step toward achieving that
goal.
Accidental injury is one of the leading causes of death in Maine and remains the leading cause of death for people under the age of 44. Uncontrolled hemorrhage (bleeding) is a leading cause of trauma death prior to arrival at a hospital. It is estimated 30-40 percent of trauma mortality is due to hemorrhagic shock, and hemorrhage plays a role in 33-56 percent of trauma fatalities that occur in the
prehospital setting.
In recent years, traffic, skiing, boating accidents, and tragic incidents of violence, such as the Lewiston shootings, highlight the urgent need for proactive measures to address emergency situations effectively. The installation of bleeding control kits in state-owned buildings is a practical and potentially life-saving initiative to mitigate the severity of injuries in critical moments.
Providing state-owned buildings with bleeding control kits with regular inspection and restocking of kits, this legislation demonstrates a comprehensive approach to enhancing emergency preparedness in
a public setting. These measures not only empower the public to respond effectively to traumatic incidents but also provide reassurance to the broader community their safety is being prioritized.
Furthermore, the provision of immunity from civil liability for those individuals acting in good faith when using a bleeding control kit underscores the importance of encouraging swift and decisive action in emergency situations, without fear of legal repercussions. The American College of Surgeons
provides free STOP THE BLEED� training through the STOP THE BLEED� program at
stopthebleedorg.
Passing L.D. 774(H.P.497) presents a proactive and practical approach to enhancing public safety and emergency preparedness, and we urge you to support this important initiative.

Thank you in advance for your consideration.

Sincerely,

Testimony in Support of LD 774 - "STOP THE BLEED�" Bill
Bryan Morse, MD, Trauma Medical Director, Portland
March 24, 2025
Good morning Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government
My name is Dr. Bryan Morse, and I am the Trauma Medical Director at Maine's only verified Level 1 Trauma Center. I am here today to express my strong support for LD 774, which
mandates the presence of bleeding control kits in state-owned buildings across Maine.
1. Traumatic injury is the #1 cause of death and morbidity in young people ages 1 to 44 years old not only in Maine but also across the Unites States.
2. Uncontrolled hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death in trauma victims. 3. The "Golden Hour" is the critical first hour after a traumatic injury where hemorrhage
control specifically has the most significant impact on survival; however, the clock starts immediately- not when an ambulance arrives.
in my role, i've seen firsthand countless deaths where simple bleeding controlwith a
tourniquet, gauze packing, or basic direct pressure in the field would have saved a life.
Because many parts of Maine are rural and there is only one level 1 trauma center, many lives are lost to bleeding during that Golden Hour where control was needed at the moment of
injury To improve survival, these hemorrhage control kits, which are simple and costeffective, should be widely and readily available to the public.
The STOP THE BLEED@ program, developed by the Department of Homeland Security and the
American College of Surgeons, has proven to be one of the most effective initiatives in immediate control of traumatic bleeding by bystanders. This legislation aligns with a growing national trend, as Maine would become the 12th state to act on such a bill. Additionally, there is growing national interest in STOP THE BLEED� as the healthcare and political community
acknowledge that trauma care begins not in the hospital, but at the moment of injury.
Our ability to treat traumatic injuries successfully depends on a coordinated response that begins with the public. By passing LD 774, you are taking a significant step in ensuring that all Mainers are equipped to help one another in times of crisis.
I would like to thank the committee for your time and for your consideration of this critical legislation. i strongly urge you to support LD 774 and help make Maine a safer, more resilient
state for all of us.
Sincerely,
Bryan Morse, MD
Trauma Medical Director

MEMORANDUM FOR RECORD

SUBJECT: LD 774 An Act to Require Bleeding Control Kits in State-owned Buildings

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and distinguished members of the Joint Standing State and Local Government,
1. Thank you for allowing me to address you and introduce my bill to Require Bleeding.
Control Kits in State-owned Buildings.
2. I belong to a family that is heavily involved in medical first response or on site
emergency trauma care. Both my wife and I were certified Combat Lifesavers while serving in the United States Anny, we count two current or former Combat Medics in the family, and we have two Paramedics and three other EMTs among our children and one of our sons-in-law. Additionally, that same son-in-law and his wife, my daughter, has worked as ER nurses. There is not a one of us who has not had to respond to some
emergency situation requiring CPR, rescue breathing or the treatment for trauma
bleeding.
3. Realizing that law enforcement were often first on the scene, many departments
around the US began requiring that police officers also be trained as Emergency Medical
Technicians and some departments are implementing Tactical Emergency Medicine units that accompany law enforcement. Gaining from lessons learned from combat operations
of the US military, multiple law enforcement and emergency medical response agencies
realized the need to update their methods for dealing with traumatic bleeding wounds. With today's technological advances in tourniquets and hemostatic agents used to control
bleeding, it is now possible to stop blood loss as a cause of death on many people from
otherwise "fixable" traumatic injuries.
4. However, like any other incident response, the true first responders are the other
people on the scene. These are most often `civilians' , non-EMS or otherwise trained
personnel who have the ability to immediately act before police or EMS arrive. This is
Why we train as many people as possible in the use of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
(CPR) and Automated External Defibrillators (AED).

5. A person can die in a matter of a few minutes from severe blood loss resulting from a traumatic injmy. A person properly trained in treating that wound and stopping that blood
loss can save that life when the nearest trained emergency response can be 10-20 minutes
away, or more.
6. That is why there has been a national Stop The Bleed campaign, developed and
endorsed by the American College of Surgeons, that has already trained millions of people in the United States, including myself.
7. Stop the Bleed Programs will not help in every traumatic injury with blood loss, but
they have the potential to save many who are injured from falls, vehicle crashes, farming
accidents, natural disasters, gunshot wounds, sporting injuries and more.
8. I want to share with you just one instance where the techniques used today saved a
life. At my last duty station, Fort Hood, Texas, I was living near the interstate at it was about 0330 in the morning. I had just walked out to my car to go make sure my soldiers were up for PT when I heard a horrendous crash. I grabbed my Combat Lifesaver Bag,
and ran down toward the highway where I saw a single car that hit one of the large light posts that was on the highway near the exit. I ran to the car to find the driver pinned beneath his wheel, semi-conscious and bleeding profusely from a wound in his leg caused
by debris from his vehicle. I fashioned a tourniquet (We did not have CAT tourniquets at
that time), packed the wound and applied a field pressure dressing. I found out later the driver was the manager at the local Applebees, had fallen asleep while driving, and did
not die because I had stopped the blood loss.
9. In order for the Stop the Bleed program to work, it requires two things. It requires that
people get trained, something the ACS provides for free, and it requires that there be
appropriate Trauma Kits to use in the event of an emergency. Just as we have fire extinguishers and AEDs in State owned buildings, this bill would provide a vehicle to get
the appropriate kits.
10. These kits would include, at a minimum, a Combat Application Tourniquet (CAT), a hemostatic bandage, a pressure dressing, nitrile gloves, trauma shears, a permanent marker and an instructional booklet and would be inspected on a regular basis in the same
manner as fre extinguishers and AEDs for completeness and serviceability.
